Kyiv: At least nine people were killed and 22 civilians injured in the Ukrainian capital Kyiv after Russia launched an intense barrage of ballistic missiles and drones overnight into Saturday, authorities said. A five-story residential building in the city's Solomianskyi District was damaged by falling debris and a fire broke out. Rescue workers evacuated 35 people from the upper floors of the building, and two people died, with eight reported injured, including two children, according to Ukraine's state emergency service. In the Darnytskyi District of Kyiv, seven people were killed and another 14 injured after the attack caused fires and damage to houses, vehicles, an administrative and non-residential building, the emergency services said. Elsewhere, emergency workers extinguished a fire in a non-residential building in the capital's Shevchenkivskyi district. There was no additional information about earlier reports by the district mayor that people were trapped in another residential building. Damage to commercial and residential buildings was reported in two other city districts. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has pressed the United States and other Western partners over Ukraine's need for more Patriot anti-ballistic missile defence systems to counter missile attacks from Russia. The Ukrainian leader late Friday said he spoke to U.S. Vice President JD Vance and discussed a meeting with President Donald Trump earlier this week in Washington, which Zelenskyy described as positive and productive. The Russian air strikes on our country continue and air defence, specifically interceptors for Patriot systems against ballistic missiles, remains a top priority, Zelenskyy said Friday in a post on Telegram. At a NATO summit in Ankara in July, Trump said the U.S. would give Ukraine a license to make Patriot systems, but he appeared to move away from that commitment on Friday during a Cabinet meeting at the presidential retreat in Camp David, Maryland, saying he had not yet made a final decision on the matter. Saturday's attack on Kyiv came just two days after a large-scale Russian ballistic missile and drone attack across Ukraine killed 10 civilians and wounded more than 50 others and saw a Russian missile enter Polish airspace. From a basement shelter where she was taking cover as a second air alarm sounded for another wave, Liudmyla Nakonechna, 64, described how she was woken by loud explosions at 130 a.m. I ran into the corridor and was standing there when the bathroom door was blown off its hinges and struck me in the leg, said Nakonechna, whose health is poor after undergoing cancer treatment. I heard the sound of shattering glass. My balcony was covered in glass, and it was completely blown apart, while the windows in my bedroom were also blown out. Nakonechna had not taken cover in a shelter since Russia's full-scale invasion February 24, 2022, but the stress became too much, she said. It's getting worse by the day, Nakonechna said. Whereas before there was an attack once every two weeks, or maybe once a week, now it happens practically every day.

https://www.euronews.com/2026/09/17/gaza.text: Gaza delivery workers pedalling through rubble on bicycles can spend 40 of their 50-shekel (€12) daily earnings fixing a single puncture.Fuel shortages, transport disruption and the destruction of Gaza's road network have made bicycles — known colloquially as "baskleet" — the primary means of delivery across the Strip.Workers who spoke to Euronews described a job that keeps them under relentless pressure: the physical strain of cycling through rubble, the cost of constant repairs, and the danger of passing daily through areas still under bombardment.In the Maghazi area in central Gaza, Mohammed Abu Amra works for the delivery company Barq.Trips he used to complete by motorbike in under 10 minutes now take him 30 or more by bicycle, with heat, rain, road conditions, and the distances involved making it much more challenging.Tareq Abu Zekri launched Barq during the second ceasefire in January 2025, then expanded by hiring workers who used their own bicycles.When he advertised for riders, 109 applications arrived within a day and a half, among them university graduates with few other options in what remains of the Strip's labour market.The company now has more than 50 employees operating across three branches in Gaza City, central Gaza and Khan Younis.Orders are transferred between areas by whatever means are available before couriers complete local deliveries, covering shop orders as well as goods sold from tents and homes.Bicycle delivery predates the 2023 Israel-Hamas war: a pilot scheme in Rafah began in March 2021, and since October 2023, bicycles have become standard as fuel has run short and vehicles have been destroyed.Repairs that cost more than a day's workAbbas Al-Souri estimates his daily earnings at between 50 and 60 shekels (€12 to €14), depending on how many orders he completes.A puncture repair costs between 30 and 40 shekels (€7 to €10). A worker who earns 50 shekels and pays 40 to fix a tyre is left with 10 shekels — roughly €2.Larger repairs cost more. Abu Zekri estimates that fixing wheels, hubs and pedals runs between 200 and 500 shekels (€48 to €120), depending on what needs replacing.Spare parts are unreliable. When a bicycle breaks down, workers strip components from bikes too damaged to ride and use them to keep others moving."From broken bikes to other bikes — it's patchwork on top of patchwork," Al-Souri said.A joint assessment published in April 2026 by the World Bank, European Union and United Nations found that around 74% of Gaza's road network — approximately 4,500 kilometres — had been classified as destroyed, with a further 13% partially damaged.The assessment put total damage to the transport sector at approximately $3.21 billion (€2.97 billion) and losses at around $1.18 billion (€1.09 billion), covering roads, bridges, vehicles and transport facilities. The figures cover damage recorded up to October 2025, calculated primarily from satellite imagery.Barq attempted to introduce electric bicycles to reduce the strain on workers. The experiment stalled when charging costs proved prohibitive: powering an electric bike costs around 30 shekels (€7) — roughly half a day's earnings.Danger beyond breakdownsOn 29 August, delivery worker Raed Adel Mohammed Alyan was killed alongside Abdel Fattah Abu Al-Eesh when a strike hit an electric bike in the Tel al-Hawa neighbourhood of south-west Gaza City, according to local reports citing medical and local sources. Three others were wounded, one critically.Alyan worked for the Hamama delivery company and was on a delivery run at the time, according to the company's director Jamil Al-Yazji.Between 40 and 50 bicycle couriers at Hamama have been killed in the Israel-Hamas war, yet around 400 continue to move packages through damaged streets and active bombardment, according to Al-Yazji.Abu Zekri said some of his workers were wounded in a strike in Khan Younis and others narrowly escaped shelling near them in the Al-Jalaa area of Gaza City.Despite the losses, both companies continue taking on workers. For Abu Zekri, the project is partly about providing income when other options have gone. What workers need to keep going, he said, is straightforward: passable roads, repairable bikes and available parts."Let us bring in pedals, half-frames, tyres, patches for the bikes," he said.

https://telex.hu/gazdasag/2026/09/20/naf.text: Menü Kereső Az ukrán határ magyar oldalán építene kőolajtárolókat a Mol és az ukrán Naftohaz Gazdaság Weiler Vilmos Állítsd be a Telexet megbízható forrásnak! Beállítom Az ukrán Naftohaz és a magyar Mol energetikai cégek memorandumot írtak alá arról, hogy kőolajtermékek tárolására szolgáló létesítményeket fognak építeni az ukrán-magyar határ magyar oldalán – közölte a Naftohaz Telegram-oldalán, amiről az MTI számolt be. Az erről szóló dokumentumot a Kárpáti Nyolcak (C8) első csúcstalálkozóján írták alá. „Az üzemanyag-ellátási infrastruktúránk elleni folyamatos orosz támadások miatt az egész piac stabilitását szolgálja az ellátási útvonalak diverzifikálása és további tárolókapacitások kiépítése a támadások által nem sújtott területeken kívül. A közös projekt megvalósítása hosszú távon nemcsak az ukrán fogyasztók számára biztosítja az üzemanyag-ellátás megbízhatóságát, hanem elősegíti az Ukrajna és Magyarország között a határon átnyúló energetikai infrastruktúra kölcsönösen előnyös fejlesztését is” – írta Szerhij Fedorenko, a Naftohaz ügyvivő igazgatója. A nemrég alapított C8 tagjai Ukrajna, Románia, Lengyelország, Szlovákia, Magyarország, Csehország, Ausztria és Szerbia. A tervek szerint a tagállamok a biztonság- és az energiapolitika terén is együttműködnek majd. A Kárpáti Nyolcak együttműködést szeptember 18-án jelentette be Volodimir Zelenszkij ukrán elnök. https://news.tuoitre.vn/french-supercomp.text: Settings Saved news Your Comment Transaction History Logout Friday, October 2, 2026, 15:47 GMT+7 French supercomputer maker Bull doubles output to boost Europe's AI ambitions Bull, the state-owned French maker of Europe's fastest supercomputers, reopened an expanded factory on Thursday to double its production capacity, executives told Reuters, as Europe bolsters its AI computing capacity. A general view of the Bull's supercomputing facility in Angers, France, October 1, 2026. Picture taken with a mobile phone. Photo: Reuters The European Union has committed €7 billion ($7.87 billion) over 2021-2027 to a network of supercomputers, aiming to close a compute gap with the United States and China. Bull's plant in Angers, France, is the only factory in Europe dedicated to building these machines, and its expansion is meant to support that goal. Chief Executive Emmanuel Le Roux said Bull has received more orders this year than ever before and has won 15 of ⁠the 18 tenders issued by EuroHPC, the EU body that co-funds Europe's network of supercomputers with member states, competing against companies including Hewlett Packard Enterprise. Airbus inaugurated Bull-built supercomputers in Toulouse and Hamburg this year in a five-year deal that had been reported in media as worth close to €100 million and tripled the planemaker's simulation capacity. A general view inside the Bull's supercomputing facility in Angers, France, October 1, 2026. Picture taken with a mobile phone. Photo: Reuters Bull told Reuters the deal value was not correct but declined to disclose the correct figure. Cloud operator OVHcloud and European Commission-backed Domyn are both attempting to train frontier-class AI models on Bull's JUPITER supercomputer alongside other companies Bull declined to name. Output could expand again in 2027 The Angers expansion cost €80 million, Bull executives said. Output has already doubled, from six racks a month previously to 12 now, and the plant can boost output to 24 next year on demand it expects to keep ‌growing. France's order ⁠from Bull, a supercomputer named after computer scientist Alice Recoque, accounts for 94 racks, and is being assembled in parallel with LUMI-AI, Finland's €388 million system and Bull's biggest-ever contract. The two orders could not have been built alongside each other before the expansion, executives said. Bull's logo inside its supercomputing facility in Angers, France, October 1, 2026. Picture taken with a mobile phone. Photo: Reuters France completed its purchase of Bull from debt-laden IT group Atos on March 31, valuing the company at up to €404 million. The original motive was strategic, Le Roux said. In the ⁠1980s, after the United States stopped shipping supercomputers to the CEA, France's nuclear agency, France turned to Bull to build the machines that were used to simulate nuclear tests. Bull built JUPITER, Europe's first exascale machine, the fastest class of supercomputers, now running at the Juelich centre in Germany. Alice ⁠Recoque, ordered for the CEA, is due for delivery in stages from the end of this year, at a cost of €554 million to the French government and European Union. The Angers factory assembles systems using Nvidia, AMD and Intel processors, or European parts, depending on customer ⁠demands. European-made components account for 70% of the machines being built, up from 20% to 30% five years ago. Under a partnership signed in June, Bull and Taiwan's Foxconn will also manufacture Nvidia's NVL systems at a plant in the Czech Republic, with final assembly in the Angers factory.
